records.query: List the classifications of controlled environments in aerospace facilities and specify the contamination control criteria for each classification.
records.reference: The classifications of controlled environments in aerospace facilities are: Controlled Area Class 300,000, Conventional Clean Room Class 100,000, Laminar Cross Flow Room Class 10,000, Laminar Down Flow Room Class 1,000, and Laminar Flow Work Stations Class 100. Their contamination control criteria are: Air flow (minimum of 10 air changes per hour for Class 300,000, 15-20 for Class 100,000, 100 ft/min for Class 10,000, 50 ft/min for Class 1,000, and an average velocity between 72 and 200 ft/min for Class 100), Temperature and humidity control (temperature and humidity control located outside the room with no manual control within the room for Class 100,000 and below, and temperature and humidity control within the facility for Class 100), and Vacuum cleaning system (central vacuum system for Class 300,000 and 100,000, portable vacuum cleaner with filtered air output for Class 10,000, and vacuum to air locks for Class 1,000 and Class 100).
records.answer:
Per TO 00-25-203, the Air Force classifies permanent environmentally controlled facilities, in order of cleanness (least to most clean), as:

1. Controlled Area (Class 300,000) – Chapter 4. Semi-clean area for equipment needing some contamination control. Operation tolerance: no more than 300,000 particles 0.5 micron and larger per cubic foot of air, or no more than 1,000 particles 5.0 microns and larger per cubic foot (automatic counter); no more than 700 particles 5.0 microns and larger per cubic foot when measured by the manual method. Air handling filtration rated 80–85% efficient NBS for 1.0 micron and larger particles; at least 10 air changes per hour. Monitored by the clean room officer at least once a month. The manual method shall not be used if an automatic particle counter is available.

2. Conventional Clean Room (Class 100,000) – Chapter 5. Particle-count criteria are in Table 3-1; the facility shall not exceed the particle requirements for a class 100,000 clean room, checked with an automatic light-scattering particle counter per Chapter 9. Table 3-1 gives 100,000 particles per cubic foot (0.5 micron and larger), temperature 72°F ±5°F, humidity max 50%. The Air Force has discontinued construction of new conventional class 100,000 clean rooms.

3. Laminar Flow Clean Rooms – Chapter 6:
   a. Cross-Flow (Class 10,000) – horizontal airflow; air velocity must not vary more than 20 ft/min throughout the facility and must not drop below 75 ft/min at any work station.
   b. Down-Flow (Class 1,000) – vertical airflow from ceiling to floor; air velocity should not drop below 50 ft/min at any work station. Both types can be maintained at Class 100. Monitored monthly for particulate, pressure, temperature, air velocity and humidity per Table 3-1.

4. Laminar Flow Devices (portable/semi-portable) – Chapter 7 covers Class 100 and Class 1,000 laminar flow clean work stations: filtration must meet the Class 100 particle count (ISO 14644-1/-2), no more than 100 particles per cubic foot 0.5 micron and larger, throughout the workbench upstream of the work piece.

Gap: The Table 3-1 particle-count values for the Class 10,000 and Class 1,000 laminar flow rooms could not be reliably read from the retrieved text, so those specific limits are not stated here; consult Table 3-1 directly.

records.query: Airflow design considerations for Class 100 cleanrooms in aerospace facilities
records.reference: For Class 100 cleanrooms in aerospace facilities, a primary airflow design consideration is maintaining an average laminar flow velocity between 72 and 200 feet per minute. Equipment must be carefully placed to avoid disrupting the laminar airflow, with operations requiring the highest environmental control located closest to the inlet air filter bank. Air locks are required at all entrances and exits.
records.answer:
Source: TO 00-25-203 (Air Force clean facility guidance). The manual does not define a standalone Class 100 room design; it states that laminar flow rooms are "capable of being maintained at class 100," and that Class 100 is achieved mainly through laminar flow work stations. Key airflow design considerations:

Facility type
- Laminar flow rooms are the only type the Air Force will construct in the future; conventional Class 100,000 rooms have been discontinued. Laminar flow rooms use unidirectional flow instead of turbulent flow, which keeps internally generated contamination from lingering in the air.
- Cross-flow rooms (horizontal flow, wall to opposite wall) are rated Class 10,000; down-flow rooms (ceiling to floor) are rated Class 1,000, but "it will be possible to maintain a down-flow room at class 100 if required." Down-flow gives the greatest contamination control over the whole work area.

Air velocity

records.query: Describe the key elements typically included in corrosion risk checklists used for Air Force equipment maintenance.
records.reference: Key elements in corrosion risk checklists for Air Force equipment maintenance include inspecting for the presence of corrosive substances like solder flux, which can trap moisture and cause circuit failure; checking for microbial presence and water intrusion, which can support corrosion; verifying the proper use of corrosion preventive compounds such as MIL-PRF-32033 and MIL-PRF-63460; and ensuring that gaskets are properly installed to prevent moisture entry. Additionally, the checklists should address the effects of environmental factors such as temperature, salt atmosphere, ozone, and other industrial pollutants.
records.answer:
The library has no single document titled "corrosion risk checklist." The closest matching content is the corrosion prevention and control guidance in TO 1-1-691, TO 1-1-700 and TO 36-1-191, plus the pre-deployment checklist guidance in TO 1-1-691. Across these, the elements a corrosion risk checklist would typically cover are:

1. **Environmental/risk factors to assess:** moisture and condensed moisture; salt atmospheres (salt-laden air condenses on equipment in early evening and morning); industrial pollutants and sulfuric oxides/acid rain, which attack coatings and rubber seals and hoses; sand and dust (which can form a damp poultice that causes corrosion); solar radiation (which chalks paint and degrades plastics and elastomers, exposing metal); and climate/microorganisms. Corrosion-prone areas include shelter skids and undercarriage, door hinges, lift rings, magnesium parts, wheel wells, trailing edges, and exposed control cables, pulleys and gears.

2. **Inspection requirements:** corrosion detection is everyone's responsibility; inspection frequency is set by the system program director/manager; the area of any scheduled or unscheduled maintenance plus 36 inches (18 inches each side) must be visually inspected; inspectors must be qualified in corrosion detection; and detailed inspections are required when damage is suspected to be extensive or severe. Suspect areas are checked with a 10X magnifier and flashlight, and with tape-lift testing where corrosion is suspected under paint.

3. **Preventive maintenance actions:** regular cleaning, inspection, preservation and lubrication at specified intervals; scheduled washing; wiping down exposed unpainted surfaces; keeping low-point drains open; inspecting, removing and reapplying corrosion preventive compounds (CPC); earliest detection and repair of damaged coatings; and using clean potable water for washing and rinsing. Water used for aircraft/equipment washing is tested every 30 days for chloride (400 mg/L max), pH (6.5–8.5), total dissolved solids (500 mg/L max) and other limits.

4. **Corrective actions:** remove corrosion, clean, and treat the surface per the cleaning and corrosion-removal chapters, then touch up paint per TO 1-1-8. Major repairs are performed at depot level.

5. **Pre-deployment and in-theater items:** complete a full wash; inspect the exterior for missing or chipped primer/paint; apply CPC to wheel wells, trailing edges, access doors and corrosion-prone areas; replace worn, torn or cracked seals and gaskets that allow moisture, sand or dust intrusion; remove standing water; unplug blocked drain holes; minimize grease to limit contaminant entrapment; and, while deployed, run a constant regimen of topcoat and CPC integrity inspection. Limit compressed air to areas where it will not spread sand and salt-laden dust. Weapon-system-specific checklists are developed by the SPD/SPO with MAJCOM corrosion functional managers.

records.query: EPTFE sealing tape applications and specifications
records.reference: EPTFE sealing tape (SAE AMS 3255) is a flexible tape used to seal gaps in places like panels, covers, and floorboards. The tape is strong against fuel, oil, water, and other aircraft fluids, and it works in extreme temperatures from –65 degrees up to 450 degrees (and even 600 degrees for short periods). It comes in ribbed and flat styles, prevents corrosion, keeps out moisture, and can be replaced easily since it has a handy adhesive backing.
records.answer:
ePTFE sealing tape (SAE AMS 3255, oil and water resistant, Skyflex) — applications and specifications:

Specification / types (TO 1-1-700 Table 12-1):
- Specification: SAE AMS 3255, Sealing Tape, Expanded Polytetrafluoroethylene (EPTFE), Oil and Water Resistant (Skyflex).
- Class 1 – Continuous Ribbed: preformed gasket tape, no adhesive on either side except as noted; no mixing, masking, or curing required. Part numbers include GUA-1071-1 (fay surfaces <1 inch wide), GUA-1001-1 (fay surfaces >1 inch wide), GUA-1001-2 (fay surfaces >1 inch wide where thicker fill is needed), GUA-1017-1 (fay surfaces ≤1 inch wide), GUA-1401-1 (fay surfaces <1 inch wide in dry floorboard areas or where thicker tape fills gaps), and GSC-21-80767-00 (fay surfaces ≥1 inch wide in moisture areas of floorboards or where thicker tape fills gaps).
- Class 2 – Continuous Non-Ribbed: GUA-1003-1 compensation (fill) tape for irregularities or minor damage repair; GUA-1057-1 and GUA-1058-1 (fay surfaces <1 inch wide) and GUA-1059-1 (fay surfaces >1 inch wide) as shim/barrier to resist minor chafing; GUA-1301-1 (fay surfaces <1 inch wide with thick gaps).
- Properties: temperature -65 to +450 °F (-54 to +232 °C), short term 315 °C (600 °F exposure noted); resists water, fuel, oil and hydraulic fluid; no corrosion inhibitors; peel strength 2 lb/in width maximum for the adhesive side.

Applications: sealing of faying surfaces, access and removable panels, and floorboards. Not for fuel-soaked or very high-temperature applications. A non-hazardous alternative to low-adhesion two-component sealants.

Use and handling:
- Use requires authorization from the equipment System Program Manager (SPM) engineering authority (TO 1-1-700); TO 1-1-691 specifies the aircraft SPD or missile/equipment SPM.
- Tapes may be ordered without adhesive for fluid-exposed areas and applied with fluid-resistant rubber cement; 3M Scotchgrip 847 or 1099 may be used to hold tape without adhesive backing during panel installation.
- Peel-and-stick procedure: prepare surface first; use compensation tape (GUA-1003-1) to level uneven flanges; cut tape to length with 30° ends at corners (no folding, to avoid triple thickness); peel backing gradually while applying; press with fingers; puncture fastener holes with an awl or scribe before installing the panel.
- CAUTION: Do not pull or stretch the tape during application. Stretched AMS 3255 EPTFE and Av-Dec HT3000 tapes will retract even when clamped between faying surfaces, and inadequate sealing may result. Failure could result in damage to or destruction of equipment or loss of mission effectiveness.
- CAUTION: Do not contaminate prepared areas with soiled hands or tools; contamination prevents proper tape adhesion.
- Do not use MIL-A-46106 silicone sealants (they release acetic acid); this is separate from the tape but relevant to the same sealing work.

Sources: TO 1-1-700 (Table 12-1, 12.3.5, 12.6.6) and TO 1-1-691 (6.3.5, silicone note).

records.query: Hydraulic Systems Safety Hazards Processing overview in Air Force technical manual
records.reference: Hydraulic Systems Safety Hazards Processing in the Air Force includes proper handling of fluids such as hydraulic fluids and corrosion-preventive compounds. All personnel must wear PPE, including goggles and gloves, to avoid contact with hazardous fluids and compounds that might result in injury, death, or long-term health hazards.
records.answer:
No page is titled exactly "Hydraulic Systems Safety Hazards Processing overview." The closest content is the hydraulic-related processing hazards in TO 36-1-191 (Table 8-2, Processing Procedures), summarized below:

- Hydraulic (MH, Level A) – MIL-PRF-46170 hydraulic oil: WARNING: may cause eye and skin irritation, may be harmful if swallowed, and is flammable. Avoid skin and eye contact, wear protective equipment (goggles and gloves), use in a well ventilated area, and keep away from open flames or other ignition sources. Failure could result in injury to, or death of, personnel or long-term health hazards. When filled to operating level, operate the system to coat inner surfaces and secure a waterproof CAUTION tag to the vehicle. If packing gland leaks develop, do not tighten the gland nut until the packing has soaked up oil (CAUTION: damage to equipment or loss of mission effectiveness).
- Inverted trailers – MIL-PRF-83282 synthetic hydraulic fluid: WARNING: may cause eye, skin and respiratory irritation, and an aspiration hazard if swallowed. Use in well ventilated areas with appropriate skin and eye protection.
- Steering systems, hydraulic – WARNING: do not mix various hydraulic fluids (could damage equipment or cause loss of mission effectiveness).

General hydraulic-related safety context: TO 36-1-191 safety precautions state that personnel must observe all safety regulations, and some equipment and chemicals have inherent hazards that cannot be mechanically safeguarded.

records.answer:
The library does not cover environmental change at the organizational or strategic level (e.g., climate policy or mission impacts). Its guidance addresses how operating environments affect Air Force equipment and aircraft:

- Climate and climate extremes: Warm, moist tropical air accelerates corrosion, while cold, dry arctic air reduces corrosion rates. Corrosion does not occur in very dry conditions. (TO 1-1-691, p. 41)
- Humidity: In Indo-Pacific environments, relative humidity is the dominant corrosion variable. Corrosion begins to accelerate above 50% RH and increases rapidly above 60%; avionics MTBF is also affected. (TO 1-1-691, p. 276)
- Tropics: Up to 100% RH at 85°F and above, combined with salt-laden air, creates a severe corrosion threat. Extended heat and humidity cause rapid metal corrosion, cracking/flaking of rubber and plastics, seal deterioration, and fungus/microorganism growth. (TO 35-1-3, p. 18; TO 1-1-691, p. 41)
- Desert (Southwest Asia): Powdery sand and dust penetrate sealed components; high daytime temperatures, humidity, UV and fine dust are the four most destructive desert elements. Temperatures in closed containers may be 100°F above outside air. Soils high in corrosive salts accelerate corrosion when moisture is present; the desert still effect causes moisture to build up in sealed areas toward ~100% RH. (TO 1-1-691, pp. 40–41, 268)
- Salt and coastal areas: Sea winds carry 10–100 lb of salt per cubic mile of air; salt fallout is heaviest within the first half mile of shoreline. Salt-laden air condensing on equipment causes serious corrosion. (TO 1-1-691, p. 276; TO 35-1-3, p. 18)
- Sand, dust, and volcanic ash: Hygroscopic, they hold moisture, affect electrical contacts and rotating devices, cause instrument malfunctions, and volcanic dust with chlorides/sulfates is extremely corrosive with moisture. (TO 1-1-691, p. 41)
- Solar/UV radiation: Degrades rubber, plastics and paints, fades colors (including color-coding on tubing and components). (TO 1-1-691, p. 41)
- Ozone and pollutants: Ozone increases corrosion rates in electrolytes and degrades rubber; industrial pollutants (SO2, carbon, nitrates) combine to deteriorate non-metals and corrode metals. (TO 1-1-691, p. 40–41)
- Temperature: Corrosion and non-metal degradation generally increase with temperature, though moderate increases can reduce corrosion by preventing condensation; some electronics malfunction at high temperatures. Mold and bacteria growth is inhibited above 104°F. (TO 1-1-691, p. 40)

Recommended mitigations in the library include pre-deployment inspection of seals/gaskets and paint, complete washes before deployment, dry cleaning of dust/sand where possible, and regular removal of soils and chloride-bearing residue. (TO 1-1-691, pp. 268, 276)

records.query: What are the seven types of USAF TCTOs?
records.reference: The seven types of USAF TCTOs are Modification, Inspection, Commodity, Companion, Supplement, Record, and Safety.
records.answer:
There are seven types of TCTOs (TO 00-5-15, Sec. 2.3): 
1. Modification – issued to modify a system or commodity by adding, deleting or altering form, fit, function or interface of a component (often called Configuration TCTOs).
2. Inspection – issued to accomplish a non-configuration-change one-time inspection.
3. Commodity
4. Companion
5. Supplement
6. Record
7. Safety

The pages I read define only the Modification and Inspection types in detail; descriptions of Commodity, Companion, Supplement, Record and Safety were not in the pages reviewed. The types are assigned Type Codes that correspond to priority (Immediate Action, Urgent Action, or Routine Action) per Tables 2-1 and 2-2.

records.query: What objects are prohibited inside Fuel Servicing Safety Zones?
records.reference: Prohibited objects in Fuel Servicing Safety Zones include active ignition sources such as open flames, sparks from internal combustion engines, and electrical arcing. Non-servicing vehicles and AGE equipment with engines not running are allowed if they do not block emergency egress. Personnel must not wear footwear with exposed spark-producing nails or metal plates. For low flash point fuels, clothing containing more than 65% of nylon, rayon, wool, or polyester is prohibited. Operating powered support equipment must be parked outside the FSSZ and at least 10 feet from any aircraft not being serviced.
records.answer:
Within the Fuel Servicing Safety Zone (FSSZ), the following are prohibited:

- Spark-producing devices are not authorized in the FSSZ (TO 00-25-172CL-5).
- Active ignition sources must be removed and kept out of the FSSZ during fuel movement. Examples are open flames, sparks from internal combustion engines, and electrical arcing (TO 00-25-172). Hot surfaces above 750 °F and the 40K loader open-flame heater are also ignition sources and are not to be used in the FSSZ (TO 00-25-172; TO 00-25-172CL-1).
- Loose metal objects that might cause sparks, such as knives, keys, or other such objects. Do not carry or wear them (TO 00-25-172CL-3).
- Matches and cigarette lighters (TO 00-25-172CL-3).
- Shoes with exposed nails, metal toe or heel plates, or hobnails. Shoes made with nonferrous metal nails or plates are acceptable (TO 00-25-172CL-5; TO 00-25-172CL-3).
- Outer clothing with more than 65 percent nylon, rayon, wool, or polyester when fuel servicing with low flashpoint fuels (flashpoint 100 °F or below). Do not put on or remove outer garments in the FSSZ (TO 00-25-172CL-5).
- Operating the Auxiliary Power Unit (APU) during normal refueling (TO 00-25-172CL-3).

Note: Non-servicing vehicles and AGE with engines not running may be parked in the FSSZ if they do not block emergency egress of servicing equipment or personnel (TO 00-25-172).

records.query: What is the minimum required timeframe for a visual check of vehicles in Level A storage?
records.reference: The minimum required timeframe for a visual check of vehicles in Level A storage is at least every 90 days.
records.answer: Vehicles preserved for Level A storage must receive a visual inspection each 90-day storage period, or more frequently depending on climatic conditions and the VFM's determination (TO 36-1-191, para 8.12.1). The inspection is recorded on AF Form 3126 or equivalent. Separately, a functional inspection is required every 180 days.

records.query: What is the difference between the packaging of garments, shoe covers, and wiping cloths as per the USAF technical manuals and orders?
records.reference: As per the USAF technical manuals and orders, garments are packaged individually, shoe covers are packaged in pairs, and wiping cloths are packaged in multiples of 10 per package.
records.answer:
Per TO 00-25-203 (clean room garments and accessories, paragraph 8.3.5), the three items are packaged differently:

- Garments (clean room garments, e.g., coveralls, smocks, hoods): hermetically sealed in clean polyethylene bags of two mil minimum thickness, and each garment is packaged individually. Each apparel package must be marked by size (S-M-L), or packed so the size marking is clearly visible.
- Shoe covers: also hermetically sealed in clean polyethylene bags (two mil minimum), but they may be packaged in pairs rather than individually.
- Wiping cloths: packaged in multiples of 10 per package. The page does not specify a bagging or sealing requirement for wiping cloths, so that part is not covered.

In short, garments go one per sealed bag, shoe covers may go two per sealed bag (a pair), and wiping cloths are packed in lots of 10.

records.query: What are the three parts of a reamer as per the USAF technical manuals and orders?
records.reference: The three parts of a reamer, as per the USAF technical manuals and orders, are: 1. Body, 2. Blades, 3. Shank.
records.answer: According to TO 32-1-101 (Chapter 39, Reamers), a reamer consists of three parts: (1) the body, (2) the shank, and (3) the blades. The shank has a square tang so the reamer can be held with a wrench for turning.

records.query: What are the Safety and equipment protocols of Military Cargo Aircraft, and how do they verify GPU/APU positioning?
records.reference: The safety and equipment protocols for Military Cargo Aircraft include ensuring the aircraft is bonded to refueling equipment, properly positioning maintenance stands, and having an appropriately positioned fire extinguisher. GPU positioning is verified by ensuring the GPU is at least 50 feet away from the fuel servicing area and within a 45-degree angle from the aircraft's nose. If using the APU, the fuel truck must be at least 50 feet from the APU exhaust outlet.
records.answer:
The retrieved pages cover safety and equipment protocols for concurrent fuel servicing of cargo/commercial and military aircraft, not a general "Military Cargo Aircraft" safety section. Key points:

GPU/APU positioning (verification):
- CAUTION (TO 00-25-172CL-2): Ground Power Unit (GPU) must be positioned 50 feet minimum, and to the maximum extent of the power cable, preferably upwind of the fuel servicing area, and within 45 degrees either side of the aircraft nose.
- If a GPU is not available and the carrier's manual authorizes it, the aircraft APU may be used during refueling. If the APU is used, the fuel truck must be positioned 50 feet from the APU exhaust outlet.
- TO 00-25-172CL-1 adds: GPU must be positioned outside the fuel servicing zone and, when possible, uphill of the fuel servicing area, pressurized fuel servicing equipment, and fuel vents. Failure could damage equipment or cause loss of mission effectiveness.
- Pre-servicing checklist items include: "Ensure GPU is positioned and connected when required."

Other equipment/safety protocols:
- Ensure the aircraft is bonded to refueling equipment, and maintenance stands are correctly positioned and bonded to the aircraft.
- Ensure aircraft stairs/ladders are correctly positioned and unobstructed for emergency egress.
- Ensure one authorized serviceable fire extinguisher is appropriately positioned.
- Ensure the aircraft is properly chocked, using MIL-PRF-32058 or equivalent chocks compliant with AF drawing 42D6594.
- Fuel hoses should be kept away from running engines and APUs, and preferably not forward of the landing gear.
- WARNING: If any tank fills abnormally slowly or not at all, stop all refueling and investigate.
- CAUTION: The aircraft settles as fuel is loaded; keep adequate clearance from stands or equipment under the aircraft.

Gaps: The pages do not describe a verification method beyond the positioning requirements above (no measurement procedure or inspection sign-off), and they do not cover a general military cargo aircraft safety section outside fuel servicing.

records.query: Do USAF's airfield vehicles require silver or black reflective tape outlining their dimensions?
records.reference: Yes, USAF's airfield vehicles require silver or black reflective tape to outline their dimensions.
records.answer: It depends on the vehicle. Per TO 36-1-191 (para 2.38), airfield vehicles operating primarily on the apron and taxiways (fire trucks, fuel servicing trucks, A/S32A-2 water truck, 463L and ground support equipment) must be marked with silver reflective tape conforming to ASTM D4956, Rolls, Class 3, Type 1, color G (Silver), or alternatively black reflective tape, PN 680 CR-85 (NSN 9390-00-948-3262). Tape is applied in 2 inch wide strips, 8 to 12 inches long, to highlight length, width and height, as illustrated in Figures 2-6, 2-22 and 2-27. Other apron/taxiway vehicles (excluding general purpose vehicles) are marked with reflective tape plus clearance lights, DOT-required hazard flashers, and the lighting specified in SAE AS25050. General purpose vehicles (sedans, station wagons, multistep panels, pickup trucks, buses, etc.) are not outlined in reflectorized tape. Separately, para 2.78 requires snow removal equipment to be outlined in silver reflective tape conforming to ASTM D4956, Type II, Class 3, Type 1, color G (silver only, no black option given).

records.query: What is the proper cleaning protocol for Airforce hoses after spray painting?
records.reference: After spray painting, Airforce hoses must be flushed with MIL-DTL-81772 Type I thinner immediately after removal from the paint gun washer to eliminate incompatible low-vapor-pressure solvents. Hoses used with catalyzed systems must be flushed immediately. Cleaning with flammable solvents must occur in the paint hangar with ventilation on. The most effective method is using a mechanical paint gun washer with solvents such as MIL-DTL-81772, Type I or II, TT-T-2935, or PCBTF, as required by NESHAP to reduce VOCs and hazards.
records.answer:
Hose cleaning after spray painting (TO 1-1-8):

1. Flush thoroughly after every use. Hoses shall always be thoroughly cleaned by flushing with a solvent appropriate for the coating material used. For catalyzed (two-component) systems such as epoxy or polyurethane, this must be done immediately after use to prevent the material from curing in the hose. (Failure could result in damage to or destruction of equipment or loss of mission effectiveness.)

2. Mechanical paint gun washer (preferred method): The most effective method for cleaning paint spray guns, paint fluid hoses, and paint pots/cups is a mechanical paint gun washer, which uses MIL-DTL-81772 Type I or II thinner, TT-T-2935 purging thinner (PCBTF), or other low vapor pressure solvents. Operate per the manufacturer's instructions; dispose of contaminated solvent and filters as hazardous waste.

3. Final flush after a low vapor pressure solvent (CAUTION): When lower vapor pressure solvents are used, the paint guns must be blown out with clean, compressed air and the lines/hoses must be flushed with MIL-DTL-81772, Type I thinner immediately after removal from the paint gun washer and prior to use, to remove all traces of these solvents. These solvents are not compatible with AF paints and primers; failure to remove them causes fish eyes and other paint curing problems. Do not use the lower vapor pressure solvents for this final flush.

Hose sizing for reference: avoid hoses longer than 50 feet; fluid hose from tank to gun no less than 3/8 inch ID; air hose from regulator to tank and tank to gun no less than 5/16 inch ID.

Note: The pages do not give a step-by-step manual hose-flush sequence beyond these requirements; the gun-cleaning steps (bristle brush, thinner dampened rag, no submerging the gun, no abrasives) apply to the gun and cup rather than the hose.

Do not use the lower vapor pressure solvents for this final flush.

records.query: What is the required distance of pressurized fuel components from ignition sources as defined by Fuel Servicing Safety Zones as per the USAF technical manuals?
records.reference: The required distance of pressurized fuel components from ignition sources, as defined by Fuel Servicing Safety Zones (FSSZ) in the USAF technical manuals, is 50 feet.
records.answer: The Fuel Servicing Safety Zone (FSSZ) is the area within 50 feet of a pressurized fuel carrying servicing component (e.g., servicing hose, fuel nozzle, SPR, hydrant hose cart, ramp hydrant connection point), plus 25 feet around aircraft fuel vent outlets. Active ignition sources (open flames, engine sparks, electrical arcing) must be removed and kept out of the FSSZ during fuel movement. Operating external power units must be parked at least 50 feet from pressurized fuel carrying servicing components and at least 25 feet from aircraft fuel vents, outside the FSSZ.

records.query: State how semi-annual safety inspections are emphasized and list the key maintenance procedures included in the AFTF technical manual.
records.reference: Semi-annual safety inspections are strongly emphasized in the AFTF technical manual to ensure safety, serviceability, and compliance with regulations. The key maintenance procedures include semi-annual inspection and operational checks, liner maintenance, locating liner leaks, cutout panel replacement, and ignitor replacement.
records.answer:
How semi-annual safety inspections are emphasized (TO 35E1-2-13-1, Aircraft Fire Training Facility):
- The Semi-Annual System Safety Inspection and Operational Checks (WP 006 00) is described as "an integral element of the general maintenance procedures of the AFTF." Maintenance is to be performed in the interest of safety and to keep the facility serviceable and operationally effective.
- The safety summary stresses that the inspection must be done by qualified personnel, and that after major repair or a major problem the owner must contact AFCEC/CXF to determine whether the AFTF must be re-commissioned.
- WARNING: If an obvious unsafe or unserviceable condition is noted, halt operations and rectify the condition prior to proceeding. Failure to comply may cause injury or death. CAUTION: The entire training facility is a no smoking area.
- If the semi-annual inspection is not conducted within 240 days, the AFTF is put out of service until the inspection is completed and documented.
- AFCEC/CXF periodically reviews AFTFs to judge the effectiveness of the semi-annual inspection procedures.
- Scheduling tip: the inspection, operational checks and general maintenance should be done at the same time as winterization/de-winterization.

Key items in the semi-annual inspection and operational checks (WP 006 00), as listed:
- Inspect burn area (level rock, drain valves, weir), burners and ignitors, mock-up and doors, dual liner leak detection point, exterior lighting, propane system, control stand, water conservation pond liner, transformer enclosure and ignitors, electrical service rack.
- Open wash-down, ignitor cooling, sprinkler and engine water valves; test water conservation pond pump operation and pressure.
- Charge the pneumatic system and check for leaks.
- Function ignition and emergency shutdown systems: flame extinguishment for internal burners within five seconds, external burners within ten seconds.
- Pressurize propane piping for one hour and check for leaks with a flammable gas detector; depressurize.
- Inspect cathodic system (if applicable), drive-around burn area for ruts and level them, and obtain a water sample for environmental testing (if applicable).

Other maintenance procedures in the work package WP 007 00 (maintenance procedures) include liner maintenance, locating liner leaks, cutout panel replacement, ignitor replacement, excavation procedures, regulator adjustment, water pump replacement, and an inspection criteria table (Schedule 1).

Note: the pages cover the procedures' main steps; detailed torque values, exact test criteria beyond those listed, and the full Table 3 maintenance schedule were not in the pages reviewed.

records.query: Can crazing be caused by the paints used in a plastic panel paint restoration process?

records.query: What is the primary method of identifying counterfeit components by USAF technicians?
records.reference: The primary method for identifying counterfeits is visual inspections, including checking for low quality or used appearance, removed parts numbers (by physical blocking or scrapping), evidence of blacktopping or re-marks, or inconsistent part markings.
records.answer: The primary method for technicians to identify counterfeit components is visual inspection. Technicians should also evaluate electronic components for indications of counterfeiting, and the most effective way to avoid counterfeits is procuring components through trusted sources (MTR Program Office or stock system). Primary visual indications of counterfeit components include: a general "used" or low-quality appearance; refurbished or re-plated leads with dents and/or bends; identical part numbers and date codes but different indents; deep surface scratches, cracks, or abrasion marks; scuff marks from re-tooling; inconsistent, questionable, misspelled, or meaningless part markings; evidence of blacktopping/re-marking; sanding scratches running in one direction; evidence of previous markings; partially filled indents; and indents with marking inside. Suspect counterfeit components should be documented and reported promptly (contact the 2M or MTR help desks and notify the chain of command).

records.query: Do propane leaks trigger an immediate system shutdown as per the AFTF technical manual?
records.reference: No, propane leaks do not trigger an immediate system shutdown as per the AFTF technical manual.
records.answer: No. The AFTF technical manual (TO 35E1-2-13-1) does not state that a propane leak automatically triggers a system shutdown. The shutdown it describes is manual: the Emergency Shutdown (E-Stop) switch must be activated when an abnormal condition or emergency occurs, such as a firefighter appearing to have blown out or extinguished the fire, failing to follow the Instructor-in-Charge or Safety Officer, falling down inside the AFTF, or entering the mock-up upright with fire operating, or when personnel breach the restricted zones. For emergency shutdown, the procedure is: activate the E-Stop (push in), close all burner control valves, set igniter control valves to off, verify all personnel are out of the burn area, purge trapped LPG from the lines, lock out/tag inoperable components, and notify the appropriate agency. The manual also says that if flames are not present within a reasonable time (15 seconds), close the burner valves and allow the area to vent before reigniting, because of the risk of explosive gas buildup. The pages I reviewed do not link a detected propane leak to an automatic shutdown, so leak response may be covered in local procedures not in this library.

records.query: Is grounding mandatory during concurrent fueling and passenger operations?
records.reference: Yes, grounding is mandatory during concurrent fueling and passenger operations. Aircraft must be grounded, and grounding and bonding wires are required equipment. Grounding wires are only removed after fueling is complete.
records.answer:

records.query: How should a user lock the old blade when changing saw blades, according to this USAF technical manual?
records.reference: A user locks the old blade by inserting a punch, screwdriver, nail, etc., in the blade hole when changing saw blades.
records.answer:
Per TO 32-1-101 (electric circular saw procedure): first make sure power to the saw is disconnected. Then, to change saw blades, lock the old blade (1) on the saw by inserting a punch, screwdriver, nail, etc., in the blade hole (2) provided. With the blade locked, remove the old blade by removing the saw clamp screw and flange (3) using the wrench (4) provided, turning the wrench counterclockwise to loosen the blade. Install the new blade (5), making sure the teeth (6) point in the correct cutting direction (upwards toward the saw). Tighten the clamp and flange screw by turning the wrench clockwise.

WARNING (from the same section): The electric circular saw produces high noise levels when in operation. Always wear proper protection to avoid possible hearing loss. Also always wear proper eye protection where flying particles may cause eye injury.

records.query: What are all of the pre-operation checks required to use the HSV?
records.reference: The pre-operation checks required to use the HSV are: 1. Set the parking brake and chock the vehicle at the appropriate hydrant outlet before positioning the HSV. 2. Conduct a briefing concerning the amount of fuel to be refueled, emergency shutoff procedures, and other emergency procedures. 3. Ensure the location of emergency switches. 4. Verify the proper grade of fuel with the HSV. 5. Remove the hydrant, coupler, and inlet hose from HSV. 6. Inspect hoses, nozzles, and couplers in accordance with TO.
records.answer:
The library does not contain a single, itemized "pre-operation check" list for the HSV. The HSV preparation steps that function as pre-operation checks in TO 00-25-172CL-5 (R-12 HSV checklist) are:

Before positioning/operating (Chapter 4, Refueling/Defueling Preparations):
- Aircraft flaps must be in the full up position on aircraft requiring under-wing fuel servicing before positioning the vehicle (CAUTION).
- Stop at least 25 feet from the aircraft, position on signal from the Aircraft Servicing Supervisor, and set the parking brake. Use wheel chocks and a spotter when backing toward the aircraft.
- Engine must remain running (idle) for the R-12 HSV; on the PAHT-750-8 HSV the engine may be shut off, but ignition must be in the ACC position while refueling.
- Shut off radio (if appropriate), exit cab, leave door ajar, and chock the vehicle.
- Ground the servicing vehicle to static ground per TO 00-25-172 and the Aircraft -2 checklist.
- Attend the briefing by the Aircraft Servicing Supervisor on fuel quantity and procedure, and ensure emergency switch and shutoff locations are briefed to all personnel.
- Verify jointly with the Aircraft Servicing Supervisor/Crew the correct grade of fuel.
- Prepare the vehicle for the appropriate servicing operation.
- Remove hydrant and aircraft servicing nozzles; inspect the hydrant coupler and servicing nozzles for security, damage, missing or broken parts, and inspect hoses per TO 37A-1-101.
- Ensure nozzle ball strainer valves are in the correct refuel/defuel position, and inspect/clean the strainer as required each time the position is changed.
- Nozzle strainers must be removed or reversed on designated defuel units; strainers are inspected/cleaned per TO 37A-1-101 on one-time defuel units before the next refuel.

Truck-filling additionally requires: position the HSV at the hydrant outlet, chock the vehicle, ground the vehicle, position a 150 lb Halon 1211 fire extinguisher (or equivalent), position and chock the tank truck, brief the operation, verify fuel grade, and inspect hoses, nozzles and couplers per TO 37A-1-101 before attaching the hydrant coupler.

TO 00-25-172 also states the fuels equipment operator uses standard checklists for the preoperative inspection of fuel servicing equipment, done before the receiver aircraft arrives at the hot refueling site, and that after pressurization the operator and ground crew check for malfunction or leaks before fuel transfer begins.

records.query: Which is the most common type of TC used in SATs, TUSs, and load TC monitoring according to the USAF technical manuals and orders?
records.reference: The most common type of TC used in SATs, TUSs, and load TC monitoring, according to the USAF technical manuals and orders, is the Type K thermocouple.
records.answer: The most common type of thermocouple (TC) used in SATs, TUSs, and load TC monitoring is Type K base metal expendable with high temperature insulation, such as Silica or Nextel fiber. TCs insulated with fiberglass, plastic, hard fired ceramic beads, or metal over braid are classified as base metal expendable TCs. Type K TCs are nickel based, with a positive lead of nickel-chromium (yellow insulation) and a negative lead of nickel-aluminum (red insulation). The maximum allowable error for TUS, load, and SAT TCs is +2 °F. (Note: the source refers to "oven" rather than "furnace" in this section.)

records.query: Required step for gaseous oxygen carts before beginning operations.
records.reference: The required step for gaseous oxygen carts before beginning operations is to statically ground the cart to a common ground before connecting the servicing hose.
records.answer:
The technical order does not name a single "before operations" step for gaseous oxygen (GOX) carts, but the required pre-servicing actions it lists are:

1. Verify the cart has a relief valve preset at 475 PSIG on the low-pressure side. Carts not so equipped shall not be used. Set the maximum pressure regulator valve to 475 PSIG when servicing low-pressure systems.
2. Statically ground the Gaseous Oxygen Servicing Cart to a common ground before connecting the servicing hose (the hose does not provide a sufficient ground).
3. Make sure oxygen servicing components are completely free of petroleum-based products (greases, solvents); examine oxygen servicing connectors and remove any traces of petroleum products before servicing.
4. Do not commence servicing if aircraft electrical systems are energized within 25 feet of the servicing operation (except those required for servicing).
5. Wear required PPE, including eye protection (goggles, glasses with side shields, or face shield) at the aircraft connection point.
6. Only qualified personnel shall operate oxygen equipment.

Also note: GOX carts with cylinders installed are considered in storage when parked and not in use, and are not required to be grounded when parked or stored. Open and close high-pressure valves slowly, opening the downstream valve first when two are opened. Use only one bottle at a time on multi-bottle carts.

WARNING (from source): Do not direct gaseous oxygen toward body or clothing; do not allow oxygen to contact petroleum products, as fire/explosion may result.

records.query: Is there a USAF-approved specification for a remover for polysulfide primer with a polyurethane topcoat?
records.reference: No. The document states that "There are no approved USAF specification removers for this finish system," but that proprietary removers have been "tested and approved" and are identified by National Stock Numbers (NSNs) for this purpose.
records.answer: No. TO 1-1-8, paragraph 2.6.2 (Remover for Polysulfide Primer with a Polyurethane Topcoat) states there are no USAF-approved specification removers for this finish system. Instead, proprietary removers of two types, phenolic and non-phenolic/non-cresylic, have been tested and approved by the AFCPCO for use on USAF aircraft, missile, and equipment metal surfaces. These removers are identified by PN and source of supply; the listed NSN is 8010-01-270-3633 (55 gallon drum). The TO recommends first removing the polyurethane topcoat with one of the removers listed for epoxy and polyurethane finish systems (para 2.6.1), then removing the polysulfide primer with a remover from para 2.6.2. Removers in this paragraph are applied full strength, with dilution, by brush or non-atomizing sprayer. Chemical removers are toxic; skin and eye protection is required.

records.query: Does the CSS hold ultimate authority in overseeing pre-operation briefings, vent monitoring, and emergency responses as per the USAF technical manuals and orders?
records.reference: Yes, the CSS holds ultimate authority in overseeing pre-operation briefings, vent monitoring, and emergency responses as per the USAF technical manuals and orders. The CSS is responsible for briefing team members on emergency procedures, stopping fuel flow, determining evacuation needs, and directing and monitoring all aspects of the concurrent servicing operation.
records.answer:
Largely yes, for concurrent fuel servicing operations, but with an explicit exception. The technical orders give the CSS (Concurrent Servicing Supervisor; TO 00-25-172 names the same role the "refueling supervisor") "full and final authority" over all phases of concurrent servicing operations and over all participating personnel, except the deployment and control of fire fighting and rescue units. Fire/ARFF deployment is under the on-scene fire chief. Team chiefs from transportation, fleet servicing, and catering must answer to the CSS to ensure their personnel comply with required procedures (TO 00-25-172CL-1).

Supporting duties in the pages: the CSS is responsible for controlling and monitoring all concurrent servicing operations (TO 00-25-172CL-4); must ensure all personnel are briefed on the total requirements of servicing, including a general overview and emergency procedures, before operations begin (TO 00-25-172); must remain in constant voice contact with the cockpit, SPR/fuel vent monitors, and fuel control panel operator (TO 00-25-172CL-1); and must ensure communications to the fire department are immediately available (TO 00-25-172).

Limits: the pages reviewed do not show the CSS holding ultimate authority over confined-space entry or the emergency rescue plan. For confined-space fuel tank entries, TO 1-1-3 assigns entry authority to the Entry Authority/Supervisor and requires coordination with MXG/CC, Safety, BEF and Fire Emergency Services, and the Emergency Response and Rescue Plan lists its own responsibilities. Also, the CSS is not required when no concurrent refuel/defuel operation is taking place (TO 00-25-172). The CSS's authority therefore applies to concurrent servicing operations, not to the overall USAF authority structure for all confined-space work.

records.query: Are Wrap Splice or Mesh Splice Procedures only used when wire replacement is not feasible for the maintenance of USAF equipment?
records.reference: Yes, Wrap Splice and Mesh Splice procedures are only used when wire replacement is not feasible, as replacement is the preferred method and the splice procedures are to be used only when replacement is not feasible.
records.answer: Largely yes. Per T.O. 00-25-259 (WP 010 00), wire replacement is the preferred wire repair method, and the Wire Repair (Wrap Splice) Procedure (para 10-5.3) or the Wire Repair (Mesh Splice) Procedure (para 10-5.4) should be used only when wire replacement is not feasible. The Feasibility analysis (para 10-5.1) directs replacement when both wire ends are accessible; a splice is used when only one end is accessible or neither end is accessible. The mesh splice is described as an alternate method to the wrap splice, and its caution states the method is used only when complete removal and replacement of the entire wire is not feasible. Note: the mesh splice is the weaker of the two splices and should not be used where mechanical stress is involved (para 10-4.2). The pages I read do not state whether the wrap splice carries the same mechanical-stress restriction.

records.query: Are emergency shutdown protocols, winterization, and fault isolation prioritized for safety as per the AFTF technical manual?
records.reference: Yes. The AFTF manual prioritizes safety by requiring configuration, testing, and certification of emergency shutdown procedures; providing dedicated Winterization/De‑winterization procedures; and including fault isolation within the manual’s scope and work packages.
records.answer:
Yes, in the AFTF manual (TO 35E1-2-13-1, AFD-100607-009), safety is built into all three areas, though the manual does not explicitly rank them as "prioritized."

Emergency shutdown: Each work package's safety summary requires awareness of the Emergency Procedures in WP 004 00, Paragraphs 7 and 8 before performing winterization, fault isolation, or other propane-related steps; failure to comply may cause serious injury. The facility has a control-stand emergency shutdown switch: pushing it IN deactivates all ignitors, closes all coaxial and solenoid propane valves to the burners, and closes the propane tank internal valve (pneumatic control). Burners have pneumatically operated high-speed emergency shutoff coaxial valves, and the propane system includes pneumatic, manual, and seismic sensor shutdown systems. The operational checklist also requires verifying that all emergency shutdown times are achieved. Fault isolation includes a "emergency shutdown not operating properly" procedure (SWP 007 01, paragraph 7).

Winterization: WP 005 01 requires that the procedure be performed by authorized personnel, that a WARNING be followed (if an obvious unsafe condition is noted, halt operations and rectify it before proceeding), and that a CAUTION be followed (the entire facility is a no-smoking area). It also requires the semi-annual inspection (WP 006 00) first, and that no vehicles be in the burn area. Winterization includes tagging and locking out ignitor switches and propane valves, and verifying emergency shutdown valves on the propane tank fill system. De-winterization carries the same warning, caution, and authorized-personnel requirements, and requires that all emergency shutdown times be achieved and a fire truck and crew stand by during live-fire testing.

Fault isolation: WP 007 01 covers electrical, propane, and water system fault isolation, with a safety summary warning of extreme temperatures and open flames and a requirement to know the auxiliary lockout switch. Procedures start with power and lockout checks before troubleshooting.

Gap: The pages do not state a general safety-priority ordering across these three areas; the safety emphasis is shown through the warnings, cautions, and cross-references above.

records.query: What is the purpose of specialized PPE in ensuring hazard mitigation?
records.reference: Specialized PPE ensures hazard mitigation by protecting personnel from toxic, corrosive, flammable, and mechanical hazards, minimizing exposure and preventing contamination. Items like goggles, respirators, gloves, smocks, and grounding straps safeguard against injury, long-term health risks, static discharge, and environmental hazards. Proper PPE use ensures controlled conditions, safety of operations, and protection of both workers and sensitive equipment.
records.answer:
Specialized PPE is the protective equipment matched to a specific hazard in a task, used to keep personnel from being injured or made ill while the hazard is controlled. The technical orders do not give a single general definition of "specialized PPE," so this answer draws on the task-specific requirements they set out.

Key points from the pages:
- Purpose: Supervisors must ensure an adequate supply of safety equipment and PPE is available and ready for issue, and that personnel use the appropriate PPE while exposed to hazardous conditions, "to prevent accidents, injuries, and occupational illnesses" (TO 1-1-700, P3451).
- Hazard-specific selection: When using chemicals, abrasive blasting, or mechanical tools, personnel must "use the appropriate PPE" and read the WARNINGS, CAUTIONS and MSDSs first (TO 1-1-700, P3451).
- Fuel tank/cell work (TO 1-1-3): Gloves are required during depuddling, cleaner/solvent application, fuel foam removal, and sealant/adhesive application. Head coverings are required where fuel exposure is possible. Neoprene booties are required during wet fuel cell/bladder entries. Respirators are generally air-supplied, full-face units, with at least three serviceable respirators connected during open tank repair. Eye protection (goggles or full-face respirator) is required where there is a risk of irritation, liquid, dust or flying objects (P2639, P2634).
- Hand creams are not considered suitable protection (P2639).

Note: The pages do not describe PPE for every hazard category, and the specific requirements vary by task and are set by the Bioenvironmental Engineering Flight and Safety.

records.query: Discuss the safety considerations when using Type I heavy-duty solvent-based cleaners during maintenance as per the USAF technical manuals.
records.reference: When using Type I solvent-based cleaners in USAF maintenance, personnel must recognize the toxic, flammable, and environmentally hazardous properties of these materials. Safe handling includes proper PPE, ventilation, fire prevention, spill control, and waste disposal. Type I should not be used in poorly ventilated areas or heated above 115°F.
records.answer:
Type I heavy-duty solvent-based cleaner (MIL-PRF-87937, Type I, a terpene-based solvent emulsion) is used for heavy oils, greases and carbon deposits. Safety considerations from the USAF technical orders:

Ventilation and heating
- Type I should not be used in poorly ventilated areas (TO 35-1-3; TO 1-1-700 notes that solvent-containing Types I/III cannot be used in poorly ventilated areas and that Type IV, which has no solvents, is usable in confined areas).
- Do not heat Type I above 115 °F (TO 35-1-3).
- Solvents must not be applied with atomizing spray equipment, which is hazardous and violates environmental regulations (TO 1-1-691).

Personal protection
- Wear rubber gloves, chemical or splash proof goggles, and water resistant boots during cleaning with MIL-PRF-87937 cleaners (TO 1-1-691 WARNING).
- If cleaner splashes in eyes, rinse thoroughly with fresh water for 15 minutes and report to a medical facility. Remove saturated clothing immediately and flush exposed skin with fresh water (TO 1-1-691 WARNING).
- Consult the local safety office and Bioenvironmental Engineer for PPE and respiratory requirements (TO 1-1-691).

Fire and ignition
- Keep solvents away from open flames and live electrical circuits or arcing sources; remove residual solvent from aircraft, engine bays and equipment (TO 1-1-691).
- Do not use synthetic wiping cloths with flammable solvents (TO 1-1-691 WARNING).
- Before applying flammable solvent cleaners, open circuit breakers associated with battery power; ground the aircraft during cleaning; do not clean on an outdoor washrack during an electrical storm (TO 1-1-691 WARNING).

records.query: What is the difference between emergency shutdown and post-shutdown procedures as per the AFTF technical manual?
records.reference: The difference between emergency shutdown and post-shutdown procedures is that emergency shutdown involves immediately pushing the emergency shutdown switch to the OFF position, closing all burner control valves, and positioning all igniter switches to OFF. Post-shutdown procedures involve closing the manifold shutoff valve, burning off all residual gas, and ensuring the emergency shutdown switch is in the OFF position. The document does not mention the activation of water sprinklers or water jackets during these procedures.
records.answer:
The library does not contain a section on "post-shutdown procedures" in the AFTF manual (TO 00-25-172CL-5), so I can only describe the emergency shutdown side.

Emergency shutdown (TO 00-25-172CL-5, Chapter 1, para 1.3): Used for hydrant-servicing emergencies. The steps are:
- WARNING: Do not actuate the engine emergency shutdown switch if the truck must be moved. Failure could result in injury, death, or long-term health hazards.
a. Release deadman control and pull the lanyard/control cable on the Type II hydrant system. If fuel flow continues, actuate the closest emergency fuel shutoff switch.
b. Actuate any emergency engine shutdown switch to stop the vehicle engine. (If the vehicle must be moved without stowing hoses, close and disconnect the nozzles and hydrant coupler, break the seal, and activate the interlock override lever.)
c. Close the hydrant coupler valve and close the single point nozzle valve(s).
d. Depart the area if instructed by maintenance or fire department personnel.
Note: Actuating a fuel emergency shutoff switch closes both the hydrant valve and truck control valve on a Type III hydrant; on a Type II system only the truck control valve closes.

Hand signals for reference: Stop or cut engine/power is a hand movement across the throat.

Post-shutdown procedures: not covered in the pages retrieved. Chapter 1 of this manual is the emergency shutdown checklist only, and no post-shutdown or restart section was found.</answer>

records.query: Discuss the cleanliness level class range required by the US Air Force contamination control standard for aerospace facilities.
records.reference: The US Air Force contamination control standard for aerospace facilities requires cleanliness levels classified as Class 100, 1,000, 10,000, 100,000, and Controlled Area (Class 300,000) to ensure appropriate air quality and minimize particle contamination.
records.answer:
The Air Force contamination control technical order (TO 00-25-203) covers airborne particulate cleanliness classes from the least to the most stringent. The permanent environmentally controlled facility types, in order of cleanliness, are:

- Controlled Area (Class 300,000)
- Conventional Clean Room (Class 100,000)
- Laminar Flow Rooms: Cross Flow (Class 10,000) and Down Flow (Class 1,000)

Portable and semi-portable laminar flow devices (laminar flow stations) are also used, rated Class 1,000 (and Class 100 is mentioned for laminar flow work stations). So the overall range runs from Class 300,000 (least clean) down to Class 100 (most clean, laminar flow work stations), with Class 1,000 down flow rooms and devices in between.

The document notes that "clean" is the contamination level just below that which affects product operation or reliability, and that specifying cleanliness above what is necessary is costly. It also states that construction of new conventional (Class 100,000) clean rooms has been discontinued, and that laminar flow rooms are preferred. Design criteria are in AFM 88-4, Chapter 5, and ISO 14644-1/-2 is referenced for classification. records.query: Outline engine start steps using a hand-held remote during aircraft servicing, and explain how to configure the R-20 remote to coordinate with the Aircraft Refueling Supervisor.
records.reference: To start the engine using the hand-held remote during aircraft servicing: (1) Turn the ignition switch to the ON position, if applicable. (2) On the hand-held remote, set the PUMP switch to START. (3) Press and release the action/deadman switch. (4) Repeat for each pumping unit required. Throttling of the engine from idle to run and back to idle will be done automatically based on fuel demand, provided communication systems and PLCs are operational. To configure the R-20 remote to coordinate with the Aircraft Refueling Supervisor, set the appropriate toggle switches (left and/or right) to the OPEN position and provide the remote to the supervisor.
records.answer:
ENGINE START USING THE HAND-HELD REMOTE (TO 00-25-172CL-4, R-18 pumping unit):
1. Turn ignition switch to ON, if applicable.
2. On the hand-held, set the PUMP switch to START.
3. Press and release the action/deadman switch.
4. Repeat for each pumping unit required.
5. Throttling from idle to run and back to idle is automatic based on fuel demand, provided communication systems and PLCs are operational.
Prerequisite: the MANUAL/REMOTE CONTROL switch is set to REMOTE and the OFFLOAD/SERVICING switch to SERVICING. The R-18 may alternatively be started manually with the ignition switch.
CAUTION: Ensure the bonding wire is connected prior to single point nozzle hook-up.
Shutdown: allow the R-18 to idle a minimum of 3-5 minutes; set the PUMP switch to STOP on the hand-held (or use the ignition switch).

R-20 HAND-HELD REMOTE AND COORDINATION WITH THE AIRCRAFT REFUELING SUPERVISOR:
- Before servicing: verify the R-20 sump tank is not over 75% full (drain below 75% first); prepare the R-20 for low or high flow; set the control valve selector switches to REMOTE when using the hand-held (MANUAL if using the control valve switches).
- Refueling Supervisor (2A3X3) gives the safety briefing, including emergency procedures, before the first aircraft arrives.
- Extend the hose, confirm the nozzle is locked (test with the nozzle crank handle in the open position) before pressurizing.
- On the R-20 hand-held, set the appropriate toggle switches (left and/or right) to OPEN, then provide the remote to the Aircraft Refueling Supervisor.
- The Aircraft Refueling Supervisor operates the deadman switch during fuel transfer and must cycle it every two minutes with a quick release of no more than one second (the control valves close if the release is longer).
- Begin pumping only on the Refueling Supervisor's direction, keeping nozzle pressure at or below 55 PSI.
- Upon completion, pumping units return to idle automatically.

EMERGENCY SHUTDOWN: release the deadman switch and activate the emergency shutdown switch on the hand-held; close the R-18 inlet valve and R-20 inlet valve (NOT the diverter valve V27); notify the aircraft servicing supervisor, operations expediter, and Fuels Service Center if possible; evacuate if directed.

Note: the pages describe the hand-held operation and handoff to the Refueling Supervisor, but do not contain a separate step-by-step "configuration" procedure linking the R-20 remote to the Refueling Supervisor beyond the steps above.

records.query: Under what circumstances is concurrent servicing not required on commercial aircraft, and who should be contacted for technical questions?
records.reference: Concurrent servicing on commercial aircraft is not required on C/KC-135 (all models), MAF, and Commercial aircraft unless loading/downloading munitions or explosives, or servicing LOX while performing maintenance. All technical questions about the manual should refer to HQ AFMC/SE.
records.answer:
Circumstances: On C/KC-135 (all models), Mobility Air Forces (MAF) and Commercial aircraft, a concurrent servicing System Safety Engineering Analysis (SSEA) is NOT required unless one of the following applies: refueling/defueling with JP-4, OR loading/unloading munitions or explosives, OR servicing Liquid Oxygen (LOX) while performing maintenance. Restrictions in paragraphs 5.6 and 5.7 still apply even when the SSEA is not required. Also, simultaneous fuel and oxygen servicing is NOT authorized (WARNING), and cargo containing explosives, oxygen, or flammable gases or liquids shall not be loaded or unloaded during concurrent servicing unless otherwise noted in Table 5-1 (cargo exceptions for C-5, C-17, C-130 and B-747 per Table 5-1 Note I). Note that the SSEA exemption does not apply to the checklist-based procedures for concurrent servicing, which must still be followed.

Technical contacts: Before beginning servicing of commercial contract carriers, the refueling supervisor must contact the commercial carrier's technically qualified personnel to provide guidance on personnel duties/positioning, discuss unfamiliar system characteristics or deficiencies, and jointly approve the timing of maintenance, cargo or baggage loading, or other activities. For commercial contract aircraft, the Simplified/Contract Carrier liaison is the SCR (Service Contract Representative), who must establish liaison with the refueling supervisor before concurrent operations to determine servicing requirements (including any unique bonding sequence) and discuss unfamiliar system characteristics or deficiencies.

Scope note: the pages address the commercial contract carrier technical personnel and the SCR; they do not give a separate general technical-questions contact beyond these.

records.query: Explain the components and design of the AFTF.
records.reference: The AFTF (Aircraft Fire Training Facility) is a fixed site simulator for realistic aircraft fire suppression training. It includes a 100-foot burn area, an aircraft mock-up with water-cooled jackets and ignitors, a water pond, and a 10,000-gallon tank for water recycling. The fuel system uses liquid propane (LPG) to simulate multiple fire types, including airframe, engine, and ground fires. The facility is managed via a safety/control stand with electrical, pneumatic, and water systems, and is equipped with manual/pneumatic shutoff valves, an E-stop switch, and fuel shutoff valves for JP-8 and propane for emergency control.
records.answer:
The Aircraft Fire Training Facility (AFTF) is a generic, adaptable live-fire training site (TO 35E1-2-13-1).

Design and history: The design was originally called the Crash Fire Rescue Training Facility (CFRTF). The original TO was dated 19 November 1996 and was retitled AFTF on 1 June 2002 when the TO went to digital media.

Major components: An aircraft mock-up, burn area, control stand, and compressor shelter. Integrated systems: liquid propane fuel, cathodic (anti-corrosion) protection, pneumatic system (including a pneumatic emergency shutdown system), electrical system, an ignition system, and a water conservation system with a holding pond (submerged and aeration pumps, an associated sprinkler, water jackets, and drain and wash-down systems).

Burn area and fuel: A 100-foot (30-meter) lined burn area with an aircraft mock-up, and a 10,000 water gallon (38,000 liter) liquid propane fuel tank. Propane is supplied to the burn area through underground pipes. The lined burn area and conservation pond provide water conservation and recycling, and the lining protects the environment from ground water contamination. For a typical scenario the burn area is filled with water to one inch (2.54 cm) above the aggregate level. Fire is ignited by 10,000 volt, 23 milliampere ignitors located in 15 burners. Switches and valves on the control stand control the fire(s).

Aircraft mock-up: Uncoated/unpainted carbon steel, approximately 72 feet long, 25 feet high at the tail tip, with a 72-foot wingspan. It has four simulated engines (two on the right high wing, one on the vertical stabilizer, and one forward of the left wing, the Engine Debris trainer). Each engine has a burner assembly and two ignitors. Mock-up ignitor wiring is enclosed in water jackets to protect it from heat. Water injection is in both wing engines and at some sites the tail engine. Wheel well and APU fires are simulated on the high wing side, and cockpit, passenger compartment, and cargo fires use interior ignitors and burners. A sprinkler system along the top of the fuselage cools and washes down the mock-up. An expansion joint at mid-fuselage allows for expansion during live fire. Replaceable 0.031 inch sheet metal cutout panels on both sides simulate emergency entry. Steel hinged doors are on both sides, and the rear left troop door is configured as the Pyrolance trainer.

Notes: Site configurations may vary by component use and location. Solenoids, regulators, valves, switches, and ignitors are consumable and must be discarded on disassembly unless manufacturer-authorized rebuild/repair kits are available. The facility is not winterized, and the water circulation system is emptied during winterization.

The pages I read do not give the full list of Design Modification Effective Dates (the table is referenced but not included in the text I retrieved).

records.query: Summarize the procedures and safety requirements for removing, packaging, and handling wet and dry batteries from vehicles; mention hazard precautions as well.
records.reference: Wet batteries (except nickel, iron-alkaline) must be removed from vehicles and reported as excess, kept charged, and maintained in a charged condition while awaiting disposal instructions. Dry batteries should be space packaged and packed in accordance with Specification PPP-B-140, with vent holes sealed. Battery posts must be protected using plastic caps or tape conforming to Specification SAE AMS-T-22085. Wet batteries may remain installed in vehicles during military aircraft transport if protected against short circuits by disconnecting and securing cables away from terminals, and properly secured to prevent acid leakage. Dry batteries pose no special hazard and may be installed in the vehicle or shipped with OVE without additional precautions. Wet batteries received with vehicles may be used until the first exercise is completed, after which they must be transferred to a battery room, kept charged, and either shipped or replaced with dry batteries. Dry batteries, whether received charged or not, can be stored in the vehicle’s battery carrier, though indoor storage is preferred, and their vent holes must be sealed until activation. Cable terminals should be greased and taped according to military specifications, and dry batteries must not be activated unless no serviceable wet battery is available. Hazard precautions include preventing acid leakage and short circuits for wet batteries, and ensuring proper handling and activation procedures for dry batteries to avoid chemical exposure.

Summary (from TO 36-1-191, Table 8-2 and Section 8.22, vehicle preservation/storage and air shipment; TO 1-1-691 for electrolyte handling):

Removal and disposition
- Wet batteries (except nickel-iron-alkaline) removed from vehicles are reported to the appropriate property class as excess, requesting disposition instructions, and must be kept charged while awaiting disposition.
- Batteries may be removed from vehicles in NMCS status only when climatic conditions or security concerns warrant it. Removed batteries must be identified with the vehicle registration number and stored in an appropriate location.
- Battery cables are disconnected only on NMCS vehicles with electrical problems or a possibility of shorts/excessive drain. Cable ends are moved away from the posts and posts covered with plastic caps or tape (AMS-T-22085 type).
- Electric powered materials handling equipment batteries go inside storage when possible; otherwise they are removed and stored on wood bases with a solid floor (two or more skids; a standard pallet is allowed if the load is 2,500 lb or less).

Packaging and packing
- Dry batteries: packaged and packed per Specification PPP-B-140 (overseas requirements). Filler-cap vent holes are plugged or sealed. Batteries are secured in vehicle battery carriers.
- Electrolyte: packaged and packed per Specification O-S-801 and stowed for easy removal at ports when maritime regulations require. For air/sea shipment, electrolyte is packed per AFMAN 24-204(1P) and attached to the vehicle under the hood.
- Wet lead-acid batteries: may be stored and shipped in the vehicle battery carrier, kept charged; shrouding is at the discretion of the responsible officer.
- Nickel-iron-alkaline batteries: may be received discharged, dumped of electrolyte and short-circuited. Discharge at normal rate to 0.5 V per cell, short-circuit each tray leaving wires connected, and keep electrolyte at the recommended level with filler caps closed. Their electrolyte (potassium and lithium hydroxide in water) is packaged per PPP-B-140 and identified to the battery type. Connector cables are preserved and packaged per MIL-STD-2073-1 and secured in the battery compartment or stored with the battery.
- Batteries secured in the carrier are covered with waterproofed protective paper (PPP-B-1055) extending down the sides and ends at least 6 inches, secured with pressure-sensitive tape (AMS-T-22085).

Air shipment (Section 8.22.3.2)
- Wet batteries may remain installed in vehicles on military aircraft only if completely protected against short circuits (cables removed, ends secured away from terminals) and secured so acid leakage will not occur. Wet batteries shipped as OVE are packed per AFMAN 24-204(1P).
- Dry batteries present no special hazard and may stay in the battery carrier or be placed with OVE.
- Vehicles are hazardous materials under AFMAN 24-204(1P); its requirements and shipper certifications must be met. Consult the Hazardous Materiel Certifier (LRS Distribution Flight).

Hazard precautions
- WARNING: Electrolyte is highly toxic to skin, eyes and respiratory tract. Avoid all contact. Skin and eye protection and vapor control are required. Have the operation reviewed by the local Bioenvironmental Engineer. Failure to comply could result in injury to, or death of, personnel or long-term health hazards.
- Wear chemical splash-proof goggles, chemical-resistant rubber gloves and aprons when handling electrolytes. If electrolyte contacts skin or eyes, flood the area immediately with water and report to the Base Medical Facility. An emergency shower and eye wash station are required where electrolyte work is done.
- Electrolyte is corrosive to metal (sulfuric acid and potassium hydroxide). Keep it off structures; place electrolyte-contaminated gloves/rags in a leak-proof plastic container; remove any battery box with spilled electrolyte before cleaning; clean spills promptly. Neutralize acid spills with 10% sodium bicarbonate solution and alkaline (nickel-cadmium) spills with 3% boric acid or monobasic sodium phosphate solution; use litmus/bromothymol blue indicators to confirm.
- Battery compartment coatings (sealant, lacquer, polyurethane paint) and isopropyl alcohol are flammable and toxic; use ventilation, keep away from ignition sources, and use acid/alkali-resistant coatings in the battery compartment. Primer TT-P-664 is toxic: use adequate ventilation, a respirator in enclosed areas without ventilation, and eye/skin protection.
- For air shipment fuel-tank preparation: static-ground the vehicle per TO 00-25-172 and have appropriate fire extinguishers available.

Note: Detailed AFMAN 24-204(1P) packing rules are referenced but not included in the library.
