records.query: List the processes in included in the Equipment Painting and list the precautions to be considered during surface painting.
records.reference: Equipment painting includes cleaning surfaces with degreasing solvents (MIL-PRF-680, Type II) and isopropyl alcohol (TT-I-735) to remove oil, grease, rust, and dirt; sanding glossy areas and removing rust by wire brushing; priming bare spots; and applying two coats of paint, allowing each coat to dry. Precautions include using PPE (eye, skin, and respiratory protection), ensuring adequate ventilation, avoiding contact with flammable and hazardous chemicals, following OSHA safety color coding, and not painting transparent shields. Items must be painted with materials that are not affected by fluids or cleaning solutions used in the machines.
records.answer:
Scope note: the closest match is TO 1-1-8, Chapter 3 (Surface Preparation) and Chapter 4/5 (Painting Application Methods and Painting Operations for Aircraft and Equipment). The pages do not contain a single section titled "Equipment Painting," so I've listed the painting-related processes from the chapter structure.

PROCESSES INCLUDED (TO 1-1-8 table of contents):
- Surface preparation (Ch. 3): corrosion removal prepaint compound for aluminum, prepaint chemical corrosion removal materials, SAE AMS-1640 solution application, surface treatment materials for aluminum, MIL-DTL-5541 touch-up, "No-Rinse Process" for aluminum, mixing and application of MIL-DTL-81706 solutions, alternate surface preparation (PreKote SP) and its use on exterior surfaces, corrosion removal and surface treatment for magnesium, surface preparation for steel, masking, and tack ragging.
- Painting application methods (Ch. 4): spray methods (HVLP, hot spray, airless, air-assisted airless, electrostatic), spray painting equipment (guns, containers, compressors, regulators, air supply, hose), spray painting technique (distance, stroking, triggering, gun adjustments), painting difficulties and remedies, cleaning and maintenance, and the mechanical paint gun washer.
- Painting operations for aircraft and equipment (Ch. 5): safety and health aspects, respiratory protection, spray booths and painting areas, paint booth types, and aircraft painting operations (depot and field level).

PRECAUTIONS FOR SURFACE PAINTING:
Surface preparation (Ch. 3):
- WARNING: Refer to Table 3-1 for minimum PPE for all paint preparation operations. Provide adequate ventilation when using solvents. Avoid prolonged breathing of vapors and skin contact. Use appropriate protective gloves and eye protection. Contact Bioenvironmental Engineering to determine need for respiratory protection.
- Surface preparation is the most important requirement for paint adherence and performance. Surfaces must be clean, dry, and free of dust, grease, oil, rust, and dirt.
- Solvent wipe immediately before primer or topcoat application, using fresh solvent on lint-free cloths and disposing of cloths as they accumulate soil (do not pull soil back from a contaminated solvent pail).
- Table 3-1 PPE examples: acid etch and Alodine conversion coating require air-purifying respirator with HEPA filter, butyl rubber gloves, goggles or face shield, and rain suit; sanding requires organic vapor/HEPA cartridges, and a PAPR with hood is the best choice for scuff sanding.

General painting safety (Ch. 5):
- Measures must be taken to prevent paint waste from contaminating air, water, or soil; disposal is directed by the Base Civil Engineer, Safety, Bioenvironmental, and Environmental Management offices.
- Painting operations are hazardous: vapors, especially in spray painting, are highly flammable, and coating materials and thinners often contain toxic substances.
- Minimum personal practices: wear approved respiratory protection; wear protective clothing (coveralls or hooded Tyvek, disposable rubber gloves, non-slip footwear) and do not store it in the painting area; wash hands before eating; do not carry food into spray areas; spray only in areas approved by Fire, Safety, and Bioenvironmental Engineering.
- WARNING: Spray gun nozzles are sources of very high pressure. Never point the nozzle toward any person in close proximity.
- Respiratory protection: at minimum, powered air-purifying respirators with hood are recommended; a respirator is a supplement to, not a substitute for, an exhaust system.
- Spray only in a ventilated spray booth; keep doors and windows closed; keep lighting explosion-proof; keep spray room surfaces clean.
- Paint booth cleaning: keep the booth and its vicinity free of dirt and dust, since exhaust suction can pull dust onto sprayed surfaces.
- Position parts so the painter is never spraying into airflow; for large equipment, start at the front (exhaust) end and work toward the air supply end. Remove painted parts from the booth once vapors have cleared.
- Paint sludge and filter disposal may be hazardous waste.

Aircraft painting (depot), when fueled with JP-8: electrostatic painting is allowed only if on-board fuel is below 100°F (38°C); aircraft must be grounded in two locations; exhaust must keep the LEL below 20% and solvent vapor below 500 PPM; an audible alarm must be installed; fire suppression must be operational; and only authorized, trained personnel may be present.

Also note: TO 36-1-191 states that the safety precautions in TO 1-1-8 apply to vehicle paint shops and spray painting of vehicles.

records.query: What are the procedures for installing, removing, and requisitioning vehicle markings, including reflective tape?
records.reference: Vehicle markings, including reflective tape, are installed by cleaning the surface, removing the liner, positioning the tape, and applying firm pressure. For removal, pressure-sensitive tape can be softened with heat and isopropyl alcohol (TT-I-735), while older tape requires paint remover (TT-R-2918) or 3M decal remover disks. Markings can be requisitioned through DLA Document Services Online. If decals are unavailable and safety is impacted, stenciling is permitted. Reflectors follow drawing B161059, mounted 24–60 inches above the ground, visible at 100 feet. Install tape according to the steps; damaged areas may be patched.
records.answer:
Source: TO 36-1-191 (Vehicle Markings), paragraphs 2.36–2.90.

INSTALLING REFLECTORIZED TAPE (2.88):
a. Clean the vehicle surface before applying the marking.
b. Remove the liner film down.
c. Position the emblem on the clean surface and tack it in place with thumb pressure.
d. Start in the center and use hard overlapping strokes of low-friction plastic squeegee.
e. Re-squeegee the edges using very firm strokes.
f. Apply clean sealer to the edges of the tape.
g. Repairs to damaged areas can be made without stripping the original tape: clean the damaged area and apply new tape over the affected area.

Specifications (2.36): Markings are reverse or direct silk-screened reflectorized tape with die-cut prespaced letters and numbers conforming to ASTM D4956, Sheets, Class 3, Type 1. Reflective red background with reflective silver letters on red, yellow, white or gray surfaces (color J). Black die-cut letters on white surfaces are for metropolitan van and modular emergency ambulances only. Letters follow Gothic style, Bureau of Public Roads Standards, Series C.
Airfield vehicles (2.38): Apron/taxiway vehicles such as fire trucks, fuel servicing trucks and ground support equipment are highlighted with silver reflective tape (ASTM D4956, Class 3, Type 1, color G) or black reflective tape PN 680 CR-85 (NSN 9390-00-948-3262), applied in 2-inch-wide strips 8 to 12 inches long, per the figures cited. General purpose vehicles are not outlined in reflective tape.

REMOVING REFLECTORIZED TAPE (2.89):
WARNING: Lacquer thinner, kylol and isopropyl alcohol are flammable and toxic. Good general ventilation is normally adequate. Skin and eye protection is required. Avoid all sources of ignition. Failure to comply could result in injury to, or death of, personnel or long-term health hazards.
- 2.89.1 Routine removal: Soften pressure-sensitive tape with heat (heat lamp, heat gun, steam, etc.). Soften adhesive residue with rags soaked in Isopropyl Alcohol, TT-I-735, and scrape away with a plastic scraper or putty knife.

- Solvents are flammable and toxic; observe all safety precautions.

On permanent transfer to DRMS or AFSVS recapitalization, AF markings including USAF registration numbers are obliterated or removed (data plates with chassis and engine serial numbers are not removed). On transfer to MAP, all AF markings are removed. War Reserve Materiel (WRM) triangles (2.87) must be removed when the vehicle leaves WRM status, but are not removed when a WRM asset ships to a contingency area.

records.query: What caution is taken into consideration while using high-pressure wash equipment, and explain the function of the portable, 45-gallon, foam-generating cleaning unit?
records.reference: When using high-pressure wash equipment, caution must be taken to ensure it is never used on aircraft landing gear and components, wheels, and brakes, as it can force lubricants out of bearings and attachment points, causing corrosion and wear problems. The function of the portable, 45-gallon, foam-generating cleaning unit is to dispense foam. This cleaning unit is a simplified, portable, pressure-operated, foam-dispensing system that uses the available air supply as its power source to force cleaning solution into the hose and create foam.
records.answer:
Cautions for high-pressure wash equipment (TO 1-1-700 and TO 1-1-691):
- Equipment developing more than 175 lbf/in² (PSI) nozzle pressure must not be used to apply cleaning compounds unless specifically authorized by the equipment System Program Manager (SPM); otherwise damage to or destruction of equipment or loss of mission effectiveness may result.
- High-pressure spray nozzles must not be used to apply cleaning compounds; use only a low-pressure soap nozzle, because high pressure can entrap compounds in enclosed areas and cause corrosion.
- High-pressure wash equipment must never be used on aircraft landing gear and components, wheels, and brakes, as it can force lubricants out of bearings and attach points and cause corrosion and wear.
- Only use approved cleaners and authorized equipment; fill only with approved cleaning compounds, use a 50:1 water-to-cleaner ratio, use only 40-degree flat fan nozzles, and keep the nozzle at least 12 inches from the surface. Equipment rated 3000 PSI / 210 °F at the attach points, and the cleaning can remove loose sealant and/or paint.

Portable 45-gallon foam-generating cleaning unit: It is a simplified, portable, pressure-operated foam-dispensing system. It uses the available air supply as its power source without pumps: air is metered directly into the pressurized solution chamber, which forces cleaning solution into the hose to create foam. The operator adjusts the cleaning compound metering valve and air valve/regulator (30 to 70 PSI) to set foam wetness. Foam is applied to the surface, dwells a minimum of one minute without drying, then is scrubbed with a cleaning kit, brush, or cloth and rinsed. The tank holds 45 gallons, operates at 40–110 PSI compressed air (15 CFM), with a 50-ft, 5/8-in ID foaming hose and a 125 PSI safety relief valve.

Safety notes: WARNING – do not service the unit without releasing tank pressure (bleed via the air dump valve). CAUTION – after use, drain and flush the tank with fresh water to avoid an extremely concentrated solution that could damage the equipment being cleaned.

records.query: Define CSO and list down the activities performed in the presence of CSS.
records.reference: Concurrent Servicing Operations (CSO) are the simultaneous servicing of fuel and other aircraft operations such as munitions loading/unloading, aircraft reconfiguration, and aircraft -6 TO inspections. The Chief Servicing Supervisor (CSS) is responsible for on-site supervision of all aspects of concurrent fuel servicing operations. The CSS's activities include ensuring all non-essential personnel and equipment are cleared from the area, briefing team members on duties and emergency procedures, checking the status of the aircraft and its systems with the SCR, ensuring cabin crew have briefed passengers, directing and monitoring the positioning of support equipment and personnel, and having SPR/Vent monitors reposition aircraft wheel chocks as required.
records.answer:
**CSO (Concurrent Servicing Operations):** The simultaneous performance of fuel servicing with other aircraft work. Per TO 00-25-172 para 1.2.8, CSO supporting Combat Sortie Generation (CSG) is the simultaneous fueling and munitions/ammunition loading/unloading, aircraft reconfiguration, aircraft -6 TO inspections, and other aircraft servicing such as oil, nitrogen, and hydraulic fluid. Oxygen servicing will not be accomplished during fuel servicing. (CSO supporting CSG is now known as ICT.) Concurrent servicing without munitions loading or aircraft reconfiguration is simply "concurrent servicing," defined in para 1.2.6 as the simultaneous servicing of fuel or oxygen with passengers on board or the performance of minor maintenance, fleet servicing, or baggage or cargo loading/unloading.

**Activities requiring a CSS (Chief Servicing Supervisor) during CSO (para 1.2.8.1):** The key function requiring the CSS is refueling/defueling. A CSS is required when fuel servicing is performed simultaneously with:
1. Aircraft -6 and -6WC inspections.
2. Munitions/ammunition loading/unloading.
3. Aircraft reconfiguration.
4. Other aircraft servicing such as oil, nitrogen, and hydraulic fluid.
5. Loading/unloading of munitions/ammunition, aircraft reconfiguration, aircraft -6 TO inspections, and other aircraft servicing such as oil, nitrogen, and hydraulic fluid.

When no refuel/defuel operations occur concurrently with other maintenance/munition tasks, a CSS is not required. A CSS is not used during ICTs; only an ATS (Aircraft Turnaround Supervisor) is used, and the ATS must be present for the entire ICT.

Note: Electrical "power-on" portions of -6 inspections are not authorized during concurrent munitions loading/unloading and fuel servicing.

Also note that the TO 00-25-172 Chapter 5 terminology has changed: the "refueling supervisor (formerly CSS)" is now used in later revisions.

records.query: Outline the exception for taxiing within the 50-foot hot refueling safety zone, specifying the engine boundary rule and the mandatory fire protection assets that must be present.
records.reference: An exception allows part of a taxiing aircraft to pass within the 50-foot hot refueling safety zone, provided its operating engine(s) do not penetrate the 50-foot criteria. During this operation, one flightline fire extinguisher must be located within 100 feet of the aircraft, and one ARFF vehicle must be in standby posture.
records.answer:
Taxiing exception: The hot refueling/defueling area is the area within 50 feet of a hot refueling operation. Part of an aircraft may pass within 50 feet of a hot refueling operation as long as the operating engine(s) of the taxiing aircraft do not penetrate the 50-foot criteria. So the engine boundary rule is that the taxiing aircraft's running engines must stay outside the 50-foot line; other parts of the aircraft (non-engine) may pass within it. Table 3-2 likewise lists 50 feet as the distance criterion for taxiing aircraft from a hot refueling operation.

Mandatory fire protection for hot refueling (Table 3-1, item for hot refueling): one flightline fire extinguisher shall be located within 100 feet of the aircraft, and one ARFF (aircraft rescue and firefighting) vehicle shall be in standby posture. The Installation Fire Chief determines positioning for optimum response. (USAFE-only notes apply per Paragraph 3.11.)

Note: The pages do not spell out the taxiing exception as a separate numbered step; the answer is taken from the general distance text and the Table 3-1 and 3-2 entries. The pages also state that for existing parking areas the distance may be modified on local conditions but not below 50 feet.
